steps.tx: A **Sprengel shoulder**, also termed congenital elevation of the scapula, represents the most frequent congenital anomaly of the shoulder girdle. Originally described by Michael Eulenburg in 1863 and Otto Sprengel in 1891, the condition arises from failure of the embryonic scapula to migrate caudally from its cervical origin (C4-C5 level) to its normal posterior thoracic resting position (T2-T7 level) during the third month of gestation.
steps.say: Sprengel shoulder or congenital high scapula is the commonest congenital anomaly of the shoulder girdle. In the third month of fetal life, the shoulder blade fails to descend from the neck down to the thoracic cage. The child is born with an abnormally high, small, rotated scapula on the affected side.

vis.title: Embryological and Clinical Overview
rows: Migrates C4-C5 to T2-T7 by 12 weeks gestation
Scapula sits symmetrically over ribs 2 to 7
Arrested high in cervical or upper thoracic zone
Severe restriction of shoulder abduction under 90 deg
Webbed neck appearance with prominent lump

steps.tx: Turn this three dimensional reconstruction so both shoulder blades face you. One scapula sits noticeably higher and smaller than the other, riding up towards the neck instead of lying flat over the ribs. A small bridge of bone reaches from that raised scapula towards the cervical spine, the omovertebral connection often found with a **Sprengel shoulder**.
steps.say: On this reconstruction one scapula sits high and small near the neck, with a bony bridge reaching to the cervical spine. That raised scapula with its omovertebral bone is a Sprengel shoulder.

steps.tx: In thirty to fifty percent of cases, a fibrous, cartilaginous, or bony bridge termed the **omovertebral bone** tethers the scapula to the axial skeleton. This anomalous structure originates from the superior medial border of the scapula and articulates with the spinous process, lamina, or transverse process of the lower cervical vertebrae (C4 through C7). The omovertebral connection acts as a rigid anchor, severely blocking normal scapulothoracic motion.
steps.say: In up to half of all cases, an abnormal bony or fibrous bridge called the omovertebral bone tethers the scapula directly to the cervical spine. It connects the upper medial border of the scapula to the neck vertebrae, locking the shoulder blade in place and preventing it from rotating when the child lifts the arm.

left.title: Omovertebral Bone Features
points: Present in 30 to 50 percent of cases
Inserts on C4 to C7 spinous processes
True diarthrodial joint with cartilage cap

right.title: Functional Limitation
points: Total shoulder abduction restricted to <100 deg
Mandatory surgical excision to free bone

steps.tx: Sprengel deformity displays high co-occurrence with **Klippel-Feil syndrome**, characterized by congenital failure of cervical vertebral segmentation. The classic clinical triad presents with a short webbed neck, a low posterior hairline, and severely restricted cervical range of motion. Other associated anomalies comprise congenital scoliosis, fused or absent ribs, spina bifida, and ipsilateral renal agenesis, mandating systemic screening.
steps.say: Sprengel deformity frequently goes hand in hand with Klippel-Feil syndrome, where cervical vertebrae fail to separate. Look for the classic triad of a short neck, low hairline, and stiff neck. Because rib fusions, scoliosis, and kidney abnormalities are common, always screen the entire spine and renal tract.

vis.title: Associated Congenital Anomalies
rows: Triad: short neck, low hairline, stiff neck

steps.tx: The clinical severity is categorized using the **Cavendish classification**. Grade I is very mild, where the deformity is almost invisible with dressed clothing. Grade II is mild, appearing as an elevated bump on dressing. Grade III is moderate, with the scapula elevated two to five centimeters above the opposite side. Grade IV is severe, where the scapula is elevated near the occiput with marked webbed neck appearance.
steps.say: The Cavendish system grades clinical severity into four levels. Grade one is barely noticeable with clothes on. Grade two shows a small bump. Grade three is moderate, with the shoulder blade sitting two to five centimeters higher than the other side. Grade four is severe, with the scapula riding right up near the base of the skull.

vis.title: Cavendish Clinical Grading
rows: Visible bump at superior shoulder line
Scapula sits near occiput; webbed neck

steps.tx: Definitive management for moderate to severe deformity in children aged three to eight years involves the **Woodward procedure**. The surgeon detaches the origin of the trapezius, rhomboid major, and rhomboid minor muscles from the vertebral spinous processes, excises the omovertebral bone, mobilizes the scapula caudally into its anatomical bed, and re-anchors the muscles to more inferior spinous processes, restoring both cosmesis and abduction.
steps.say: For moderate to severe deformity in children aged three to eight years, the Woodward procedure is the operation of choice. The surgeon detaches the trapezius and rhomboid muscles from the spine, cuts out the tethering omovertebral bone, slides the scapula downward into place, and stitches the muscles down to lower vertebrae, restoring shoulder motion.

left.title: Woodward Operation Steps
points: Subperiosteal detachment of trapezius and rhomboids
Resection of prominent superomedial scapular angle

right.title: Green Procedure Alternative
points: Traction wire to lower rib or latissimus
High risk of brachial plexus traction palsy

quiz.q: What is the embryological failure that results in a Sprengel shoulder?
options: Failure of the embryonic scapula to descend caudally from the cervical region
Premature fusion of the coracoid and acromial secondary ossification centers
Avascular necrosis of the glenoid labrum during the second trimester
Complete failure of clavicular intramembranous ossification
quiz.explain: Sprengel shoulder results from the failure of the scapula to complete its normal caudal descent from the C4-C5 level down to the T2-T7 thoracic wall during the 9th to 12th weeks of gestation.

quiz.q: What anomalous anatomical structure bridges the scapula to the cervical spine in 30 to 50 percent of Sprengel shoulder cases?
quiz.explain: The omovertebral bone (or cartilaginous/fibrous bar) connects the superior medial angle of the scapula to the cervical spinous processes (C4-C7) in 30 to 50 percent of cases.
